articles.title: This remarkable new material could solve a major carbon capture problem
articles.summary: Scientists have developed a new carbon capture material that turns moisture from an obstacle into an advantage, potentially solving a major problem with removing CO2 from industrial emissions. The material works even in extremely humid conditions and can be reused repeatedly, offering a promising path toward cheaper, more effective carbon capture.
articles.content:
A newly developed material from Oregon State University could help solve one of the biggest challenges in industrial carbon capture: removing carbon dioxide from emissions that contain large amounts of water vapor. Instead of allowing moisture to interfere with the process, the material uses it to help maintain effective carbon capture.

The researchers have filed a patent application for the innovation, which belongs to a class of materials known as metal-organic frameworks, or MOFs. Their findings, published in Angewandte Chemie, could help make carbon capture more practical and affordable for factories and other industrial facilities.

The advance could have important implications for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Industrial operations, including the burning of fossil fuels to produce energy, are major sources of atmospheric carbon dioxide. In the United States, industry accounts for 30% of total greenhouse gas emissions, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.

A New Material That Overcomes a Major Carbon Capture Problem

The new material, called BVR-X, has an unusual internal structure that keeps water and carbon dioxide largely separated within its microscopic pores. By directing the two substances into different regions, it prevents water molecules from occupying the spaces needed to capture carbon dioxide.

"This internal organization helps the material work under conditions that more closely resemble real industrial emissions," said Kyriakos Stylianou, professor of chemistry in the OSU College of Science.

MOFs are crystalline materials built from positively charged metal ions connected by organic molecules called ligands, which act as linkers. The metal ions form connection points, or nodes, while the linkers join them together into repeating structures resembling tiny cages. These structures contain extremely small pores that can trap gas molecules on their internal surfaces through a process called adsorption, much like a sponge holds substances within its structure.

One of the advantages of MOFs is their remarkable adaptability. Scientists can combine different metals and organic linkers to create materials with specific characteristics. According to Stylianou, millions of MOF designs are theoretically possible. Researchers have already synthesized more than 100,000 distinct MOFs and predicted the properties of hundreds of thousands more.

Why Carbon Capture Needs Better Materials

"The capture of CO 2 is critical for meeting net-zero emission targets," said Stylianou, who directs OSU's Materials Discovery Laboratory, known as the MaD Lab. "MOFs have shown a lot of promise because of their porosity and their structural versatility."

Carbon dioxide is a major greenhouse gas released when fossil fuels are burned. As it accumulates in the atmosphere, it traps heat and contributes to global warming.

One approach to addressing the problem involves removing carbon dioxide directly from the atmosphere. Facilities designed for this purpose are beginning to operate in different parts of the world. The world's largest such plant opened in Iceland in 2024, although its annual carbon removal capacity is still relatively small compared with global emissions. According to Stylianou, the facility can capture roughly as much carbon dioxide in one year as about 7,200 cars produce over the same period.

Capturing carbon dioxide before it reaches the atmosphere is another option, and the technologies used for this purpose are considerably more established. At factories and power plants, carbon capture systems can intercept emissions as they travel through exhaust systems and smokestacks. Some of these systems use MOFs to adsorb carbon dioxide molecules from the passing gases.

How Water Makes Industrial Carbon Capture Difficult

A major obstacle, however, is that industrial exhaust often contains substantial amounts of water vapor. Many MOFs that perform well in controlled laboratory experiments lose much of their carbon capture ability when exposed to the humid conditions found in actual smokestacks.

The gases can be dried before carbon dioxide is removed, but doing so requires additional equipment and energy. Those costs can become so significant that the overall process is no longer economically practical for industrial use.

BVR-X offers a different approach. Rather than requiring moisture to be removed, the material responds to water in a way that preserves its ability to collect carbon dioxide. Its internal organization allows water and carbon dioxide to occupy different regions, helping prevent the competition that normally undermines carbon capture performance.

"Water usually makes capturing carbon dioxide more difficult," he said. "Our new material does something unusual: It responds to water by changing in a way that lets it keep capturing CO 2 effectively even under very humid conditions."

Strong Performance Under Realistic Industrial Conditions

Laboratory tests demonstrated that BVR-X could efficiently capture carbon dioxide from a highly humid gas stream containing only 4% carbon dioxide.

That concentration is particularly relevant to emissions from burning natural gas, where carbon dioxide makes up a relatively small proportion of the exhaust. Extracting it becomes especially difficult when large quantities of water vapor are also present.

The experiments therefore tested the material under conditions that resemble an important real-world challenge, "where separating a small amount of CO 2 in the presence of substantial water is particularly challenging," said Stylianou.

The researchers also found that BVR-X could repeatedly capture and release carbon dioxide without losing its effectiveness over dozens of cycles. This ability to regenerate the material is important because commercial carbon capture systems must reuse their capture materials many times to keep operating costs manageable.

"And the material can be regenerated and reused, maintaining performance through dozens of capture-and-release cycles and tolerating demanding conditions," he added. "Those are important qualities for practical carbon-capture technologies."

The results suggest that BVR-X could help overcome a major limitation of existing MOF technologies, particularly in industrial settings where removing moisture from exhaust gases would otherwise be costly.

Research Team and Funding

The study brought together researchers from several institutions. Stylianou worked with MaD Lab members Ankit Yadav, Emmanuel Musa and Andrzej Gładysiak, along with Micah Hickethier, Chun-Wai Chang and Kai Shen Choong from the Oregon State College of Engineering.

Additional collaborators included scientists from the University of California, Berkeley; the University of Oregon; and the ARAMCO Research and Development Center.

Funding was provided by Saudi Aramco, the Murdock Charitable Trust, and a donor-advised fund established by Oregon State University alumni and retired public school teachers Brian and Marilyn Kleiner through the OSU Foundation.

articles.personality_title: New material captures carbon dioxide even in humid industrial gases

**Context** – Factories and power plants release carbon dioxide (CO2), a gas that warms the planet. Removing CO2 from their emissions is hard because these gases often have lots of water vapor, which stops many materials from capturing CO2 effectively.

**What happened** – Scientists at Oregon State University created a new material called BVR-X that can capture CO2 even when there is a lot of moisture. This material, part of a group called metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), keeps water and CO2 separate inside tiny pores, so water does not block CO2 capture. The team tested BVR-X in the lab with gas similar to real industrial emissions and found it works well and can be used over and over.

**Impact** – BVR-X solves a big problem in carbon capture by using moisture as a help instead of a hindrance. This could make capturing CO2 from factories cheaper and more practical, helping reduce a large source of greenhouse gases. Since industry causes about 30% of U.S. emissions, this advance could make a real difference in cutting pollution.

**What's next step** – The researchers have applied for a patent and will likely work on scaling up the material for real industrial use. If successful, BVR-X could be added to carbon capture systems in factories worldwide to improve their efficiency and lower costs.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new material from Oregon State University can capture carbon dioxide effectively even in very humid industrial gases, offering a promising way to reduce emissions from factories.

articles.title: The Greek coastline cleanup that turned trash into a pollution map
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM At some point in the past three decades, a beer can printed with a Spanish-language ad for a 1990s World Cup washed up on Patroklos, a small islet in the Saronic Gulf about 65 nautical miles (75 miles) from Athens. No swimmer left it there. Like most of what […]
The post The Greek coastline cleanup that turned trash into a pollution map first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

At some point in the past three decades, a beer can printed with a Spanish-language ad for a 1990s World Cup washed up on Patroklos, a small islet in the Saronic Gulf about 65 nautical miles (75 miles) from Athens. No swimmer left it there. Like most of what collects on Greece’s harder-to-reach shores, it rode in on the currents, and it stayed until a crew working on a Greek coastline cleanup picked it up, sorted it, and wrote it down. That last step, the writing down, is what makes this project more interesting than a beach sweep. Every bottle, net, and wrapper the crew logs becomes a clue about where the Mediterranean’s waste starts its trip.

A Greek coastline cleanup run from the sea

The Typhoon and its 20-person crew

Greece has the longest coastline of any Mediterranean country, and much of it has no road leading to it. Since July 2019, the Typhoon Project has reached those stretches by water, using a 72-meter (236-foot) ship as its base. Each day, a crew of 20 heads ashore in five inflatable boats and gathers, sorts, and records between 500 and 1,000 kilograms (roughly 1,100 to 2,200 pounds) of waste, which then goes to the appropriate facilities for recycling.

The project belongs to the Public Benefit Foundation Athanassios C. Laskaridis, a Greek foundation whose work centers on protecting the environment and the sea in particular. By February 2023, the crew had completed its first full circuit of the islands and most of the mainland coast.

Seven years, 1,140 tonnes

Across more than 10,000 cleanup operations, the Typhoon has removed 1,140 tonnes (about 1,257 US tons) of trash. Peggy Xirotagarou, the foundation’s executive director, has learned that the number means more to people as an image than as a weight. “To help people picture it in their minds, we are talking about 22 Olympic-size swimming pools or around 1160 large containers,” she said.

Marine litter as a research record

Counting every item on every beach

The cleanup is half the job. The other half happens after the bags are on board, when the crew records what was found, item by item and beach by beach. Thanasis Besios, who manages the Typhoon Project, considers that record as valuable as the cleared sand. “One part of the project is collecting the waste, but the second is collecting the data. We carry out detailed recording of all the waste. We know exactly what quantity there is, how many kilos, how many items from each beach. At the moment we have the largest database on marine pollution in the Mediterranean, and we are developing it every day,” he told Euronews.

Researchers are putting that record to use. The project works with the Laboratory of Marine Geology and Physical Oceanography at the University of Patras to study waste on the seabed of the Saronic and Thermaic Gulfs, and with the Marine Remote Sensing Research Group at the University of the Aegean, which uses remote sensing technology to locate and map plastics.

Tracing coastal pollution back inland

The Cyclone program

Seven years of sorting led the foundation to an uncomfortable conclusion about its own beaches. Plenty of what lands on the coast was never thrown into the sea in the first place, and illegal, unmanaged landfills are still running in many parts of Greece. “By observing the waste we were finding on the shores, we realised that a large proportion came from inland,” Xirotagarou said. The foundation’s response, launched in 2024, is a land-based counterpart called Cyclone. “It involves large-scale clean-ups in lakes, rivers and archaeological sites. We have created three large teams in different parts of Greece, where every day we collect more than 1,000 kilos of waste,” she said.

Schools on every stop

Wherever the Typhoon drops anchor, the team also visits local schools, then brings students out to the shoreline. Xirotagarou sees the classroom work as the long game behind the whole operation. “Because that is the ultimate goal. For them to become responsible citizens and for this reckless use of single-use plastics to stop,” she said.

A project that began by picking up after the sea has ended up asking where the trash started. A crew can clear an islet in an afternoon, but slowing what reaches it depends on the steadier work the foundation has added since 2024, from the river and lake crews to the classroom visits. The Greek coastline cleanup will keep finding cans like the one on Patroklos, though its logbook now gives Greece a much clearer sense of which ones drifted in from abroad and which started a few miles inland.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.
articles.source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

articles.personality_presentation_es:

articles.title: How measuring the state of nature can reverse biodiversity loss
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03714-8A collective effort by governments, communities and businesses to track the impacts of conservation and restoration is essential to maintaining nature and the services it provides.
articles.content:
Biodiversity is the cornerstone of human survival — providing us with food, shelter, medicines, clean air and water, and contributing to our general well-being. Its continuing loss is a major risk to us and to the global economy.

To build a better world, stop chasing economic growth

Extreme degradation of ecosystems is projected to cost the world at least US$2.7 trillion, or 2.3% of global gross domestic product, each year by 20301. That’s almost three times more than the annual cost of protecting nature (up to $967 billion)2, a figure that happens to be similar to the amount governments paid in 2024 to subsidize the fossil-fuel industry ($920 billion; see go.nature.com/4ejtafn).

Those stark numbers should drive efforts to protect nature. In 2022, the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework set out an ambitious pathway to reach the vision of a world living in harmony with nature by 20503. But what’s missing is a way to measure progress. A systematic approach to tracking biodiversity losses and attempts to reverse them is urgently needed.

The Nature Positive Initiative (NPI) has begun to do this by developing metrics to record the ‘state of nature’. Launched in 2023, the NPI is a consortium of the world’s largest sustainable business and finance coalitions and conservation organizations.

Cities and countryside are intimately linked — green initiatives must recognize that

The metrics aim to provide a globally consistent minimal framework — a simple common language — for tracking changes in nature across countries and sectors. They were developed through a consensus process and measure ecosystem extent and condition, species extinction risks and population trends across terrestrial, freshwater and marine realms4.

They are also designed to integrate with existing global standards and frameworks for reporting and disclosing nature-related financial risks, such as the Science Based Targets Network (SBTN)5 and the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD)6. This compatibility increases the likelihood that scientifically sound metrics will be reported and embedded by businesses and financial institutions in their disclosures and policies, and in systems for risk management and investment — all of which are essential to decision-making.

So far, the metrics have been tested with 29 companies across 23 countries at more than 50 sites. However, they still need rigorous, independent assessment in real-world contexts to ascertain whether they are practical to implement and really improve environmental outcomes. Without empirical validation, there is a risk that these nature metrics might generate misleading signals to investors, fail to detect meaningful ecological change or impose monitoring cost burdens that limit the uptake of biodiversity projects.

Here we highlight four challenges and a way forward.

Room for confusion

Although they are called metrics, the NPI measures are in fact a broad framework of indicators and recording approaches. Their focus on assessing the broad ‘state’ of ecosystems, rather than concentrating on the pressures on nature or actions for protection, is an important shift. It moves companies away from simply reporting their activities, instead making them and others accountable for outcomes. But it leaves latitude in how organizations will interpret and apply the metrics, potentially weakening their overall impact.

For example, the metrics have three levels of detail or precision — preparatory, medium and high — to recognize the uneven global distribution of data, expertise and resources. Although this flexibility makes them easier to apply in diverse settings, it creates challenges for comparability and interpretation when assessments are undertaken on different spatial scales or levels of precision.

The Tiaozini wetlands in eastern China are a crucial ecological hub.Credit: Costfoto/NurPhoto via Getty

The idea is that companies will get on board early with the preparatory level of precision and then progress towards more high-quality, ecologically meaningful measures and outcomes. A preparatory-level assessment might use data with relatively coarse spatial resolution and classify land cover as natural or not natural, for instance. More-advanced assessments would have higher resolution and use more-precise ecosystem classifications.

The concern is that organizations might cherry-pick ‘easy’ ecosystem characteristics or species to measure, potentially biasing their reporting towards apparent gains rather than describing those that are meaningful. For instance, common species are more likely to respond well to ecological improvements than specialist species are, even though the specialists might be a higher priority for conservation.

Over-reporting of improvements, particularly in relation to ecosystem connectivity and extent, can provide a misleading sense of how well species can survive genetic and demographic challenges. Better understanding of these measures is also important in guarding against changes that might not only bring benefits but also could do harm, such as when connectivity promotes the movement of invasive species that alter the local ecosystem.

Accounting for natural complexity

Another challenge is that nature is forever changing through a myriad of interactions between living species and the environment, as well as with shifting global processes such as climate change. With simple metrics, there is a risk that complex, dynamic processes and non-linear changes will be missed and the damages and risks underestimated.

How biodiversity credits could help to conserve and restore nature

Measuring the number of hectares restored, for instance, can indicate where conservation action has occurred, but not whether nature has recovered, ecosystem functions have been reinstated or threatened species populations are increasing.

The inclusion of ecosystem condition and species status measures in the NPI metrics aim to address this complexity. But this will work only if they are not simplified to the point at which they no longer provide an accurate and comprehensive assessment of how a site is changing.

Global comparability versus local needs

Reconciling the tension between a global approach for nature impacts and the local ecological and sociopolitical experiences of these impacts is challenging. Although global consistency is essential for corporate reporting so that investors can make informed comparisons, at the local level, biodiversity protection and the financial impacts and dependencies of communities on natural resources are inherently context-specific. Metrics designed to support global comparisons between organizations might overlook ecological, cultural and social values that are important locally.

Why environmental treaties must also address mental health

Many users of the state of nature metrics and global biodiversity frameworks will draw heavily on global data sets. Such resources include the Global Forest Watch Open Data Portal and the Copernicus Global Dynamic Land Cover product for ecosystem extent and condition, and the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species as a proxy for species that are at risk of extinction.

But without on-the-ground verification, the metrics will fail, particularly in data-poor regions, by misrepresenting fine-scale ecological conditions and changes. Relying on remote-sensing products that describe only the tree canopy, for example, can miss much about the structure of the forest below. Indigenous knowledges might also be disregarded. Overlooking local values and knowledge is concerning because it reinforces the broader global pattern of marginalizing local communities in environmental decision-making.

Implementation, incentives and impact

Implementation of the metrics and the incentives behind them that push companies to engage with nature measurement are likely to have both positive and negative impacts on nature and communities. What these impacts look like is currently unknown. This is why the metrics need to be independently tested to assess their value for nature, businesses and communities.

Impacts on nature will be driven by how priority species are determined, how the metrics are combined and compared and the time frame in which changes will be measured. For example, should equal weight be given to population change in critically endangered species and to species of important cultural value to local communities?

And how should users compare shifts in the components of an ecosystem that typically change over decades (such as growth of a forest) to those that develop much more rapidly (such as the life cycles of pollinating insects)? Developing guidance on how to grapple with these complexities will be essential if the metrics are to describe the state of nature.

articles.personality_title: New global system helps track and protect nature’s health
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Biodiversity, the variety of life on Earth, provides humans with food, clean air, medicine, and more. But it is disappearing fast, threatening both nature and the economy. To stop this, many countries agreed in 2022 to work toward a world where people live in harmony with nature by 2050. However, they lacked a clear way to measure progress.

**What happened** – In 2023, the Nature Positive Initiative (NPI) was launched. It brings together big businesses, financial groups, and conservation experts to create a common set of measurements for the ‘state of nature.’ These measurements check the size and health of ecosystems, risks to species, and population trends in forests, rivers, and oceans. So far, 29 companies in 23 countries have tested these tools.

**Impact** – This new system is important because it gives everyone a simple way to see if nature is improving or getting worse. It moves beyond just reporting activities and focuses on actual results. The metrics also connect with other global rules used by businesses and investors, making it easier to include nature’s health in financial decisions. Still, the system faces challenges, like making sure the data is accurate everywhere and respects local environments and cultures.

**What’s next step** – The NPI’s measurements need to be tested more in real-world situations to make sure they work well and truly help nature. Researchers will also work on clear guidance to handle complex natural changes and balance global comparisons with local needs. This will help companies and governments use the system effectively to protect biodiversity.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new global framework is creating clear, shared ways to measure and improve the health of nature, helping efforts to stop biodiversity loss worldwide.

articles.title: COP31 enters decisive week as climate talks face political test and AI initiatives gather pace
articles.summary: New international initiatives on artificial intelligence and green industrialization showcased technology’s growing role in climate action, even as negotiators remained deadlocked on finance, fossil fuels and adaptation ahead of the final stretch of the UN talks.
articles.content:
Today at COP31

Negotiations: Ministers prepare for the high-level segment as pressure mounts over finance, fossil fuels and a possible overarching agreement.

Ministers prepare for the high-level segment as pressure mounts over finance, fossil fuels and a possible overarching agreement. Artificial intelligence: A new Antalya pledge attracts 80 endorsements and 271 commitments to make AI more sustainable.

A new Antalya pledge attracts 80 endorsements and 271 commitments to make AI more sustainable. Green industrialization: Governments launch an initiative to accelerate investment in cleaner steel, cement and other industrial products.

Governments launch an initiative to accelerate investment in cleaner steel, cement and other industrial products. Science: Countries remain divided over when the next major Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) climate assessment should be published, with vulnerable nations pushing for a 2028 deadline.

As COP31 entered its second and final week, the corridors of the conference centre in Antalya, Türkiye, began filling up again, with ministers arriving ahead of Tuesday's formal high-level segment after seven days dominated by technical negotiations, announcements and speeches.

And there is plenty awaiting them.

Countries remain divided over who should pay for climate action, how to help vulnerable nations adapt, how to protect workers during the energy transition and what the final agreement should say about moving away from fossil fuels.

Late Monday, Australia, COP31 co-host and lead negotiator, circulated a first draft of the overarching decision, but the text remains only a starting point for negotiations. Countries are divided not only over its contents, but over whether such a decision should exist at all.

Soundcloud

Ministers will gather in a Divan, an Ottoman term for an imperial assembly, to seek political compromises on the most contentious issues still dividing countries.

A ‘slow first half’ with the toughest decisions ahead

For Soenke Kreft, a climate policy expert at the United Nations University, the negotiations resemble a football match heading into its second half.

“We probably will also have overtime,” he told UN News.

While some technical issues have been resolved, much of the political work remains unfinished.

“It has been a somewhat slow first half,” he said. “We really need to see a momentum swing for the second week.”

One example is a growing dispute over science itself. Countries remain divided over when the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) should publish its next major assessment, with vulnerable nations pushing for the findings to be ready in 2028, in time to inform the second Global Stocktake, which will assess global progress under the Paris Agreement.

The deadlock has delayed decisions on the scientific timetable, raising concerns that governments could enter future negotiations without the latest comprehensive findings on climate change.

“We have to defend science. We have to defend the scientists,” said Laurence Tubiana, CEO of the European Climate Foundation and one of the architects of the Paris Agreement, at a packed science plenary on Monday.

UN News/Laura Quiñones

Mary Robinson, former President of Ireland, echoed her concerns: “The world cannot afford to undermine or lose the IPCC,” urging countries to resolve their differences and ensure its next assessment is delivered on time.

Scientists also warned about the risks of overshoot – temporarily exceeding the 1.5°C warming threshold – and called for the latest evidence to guide decisions at COP31.

Activists warn against distractions

Meanwhile, climate activists spoke against allowing the proposed overarching decision to distract from negotiations on concrete climate action.

“Cover decisions, at the end of the day, have the danger of becoming a distraction,” a Climate Action Network representative said, urging journalists to look beyond political declarations.

The group criticized proposals for a just transition mechanism that would give workers and communities a voice without providing the necessary resources.

One activist compared it to being offered “a seat at the table with no food, no place, no cutlery, and very bad wine.”

“The coal miners in Australia, the lithium, cobalt, platinum miners in Africa, the steel workers in Germany, India and UK cannot afford more dialogues,” he added.

© UNU-EHS/Austin Gonzales

On finance, activists questioned how major climate funds would be replenished, noting that the Solomon Islands, a climate-vulnerable small island nation, was the first country to announce a contribution to the Green Climate Fund at COP31 while commitments from wealthier countries remained scarce

Can AI help the climate without making it worse?

Artificial Intelligence can help predict extreme weather, identify vulnerable communities and improve energy efficiency. But increasingly powerful models also require vast amounts of electricity and water.

At a ministerial meeting, Türkiye and the UN International Telecommunication Union (ITU) launched the Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge, which had secured 80 endorsements and 271 commitments by Monday morning.

The voluntary initiative seeks to reduce AI’s environmental footprint through cleaner energy, more efficient infrastructure, better emissions tracking and wider access to technology, particularly in developing countries.

Tweet URL

ITU Deputy Secretary-General Tomas Lamanauskas warned that energy consumption from data centres powering AI is expected to double by 2030, while some technology companies have already seen their emissions rise by 50 per cent in recent years.

“This is becoming a challenge that we need to rein in if we want [...] to make sure that AI is a solution, not the problem,” he said.

He stressed that the real test of the Antalya Pledge would be its implementation, with the ITU committing to track progress and hold participants accountable.

From climate risks to practical solutions

For Álvaro Rojas of the United Nations University in Bonn, AI is already helping governments make better decisions. His team used it to analyse 1,600 disaster risk management documents, identifying where countries need support on climate-related loss and damage and where expertise already exists.

“Technology is a tool,” he told UN News. “The tool itself is only useful as long as the people understand what is behind it.”

But AI also carries risks. A UNESCO-University College London study found chatbots sometimes abandon established climate facts when challenged, while accuracy varies across languages.

The findings reinforce concerns behind a joint UN, Brazil and UNESCO initiative to protect the integrity of climate information, particularly during disasters.

One new project is attempting to address that problem using AI itself.

Brigitte Perrin, founder of Earth Info Hub and former UN official, is developing Beluga, an AI platform designed to bring trusted scientific information together.

© Briggite Perrin

“All the science that the UN organizations, the scientific organizations are creating, day after day, they tend to be spread and fragmented into several platforms and websites,” she explained.

The aim, she said, is to create “a central place and safe place” where policymakers, journalists and the public can find reliable environmental research.

Cleaning up the industries that built the modern world

Beyond AI, another focus at COP31 was how to make the steel, cement and other industries underpinning modern life less polluting.

At a ministerial meeting, governments launched the Antalya Green Industrialization Compact, an initiative aimed at unlocking investment, creating markets for cleaner industrial products and helping developing countries access new technologies.

“Green industrialisation is about turning the momentum in renewable energy into industrial opportunity that creates jobs, attracts investment, and strengthens energy security,” said Ciyong Zou, Deputy Director-General of the UN Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO).

Michael Apicelli, head of the Climate Club Secretariat, a coalition of 53 countries working to cut industrial emissions, said many of the solutions are already within reach.

“This isn’t some kind of new technology we're all waiting around for. It’s here. These technologies are here today. The investments just need to be made,” he told UN News.

The urgency, he explained, is that investments in steel and cement production can lock in technologies for 30 to 40 years, making today's choices critical for future generations.

So, what would cleaner industry actually look like?

Peter Schniering, founder of Future Cleantech Architects, a Germany-based non-profit think tank focused on climate innovation, pointed to smarter building designs that use less concrete and steel, and electric furnaces that can reduce emissions from steelmaking.

© UNU-EHS/Austin Gonzales

“We have way more efficient ways to design buildings and then also to use more low carbon building materials,” he said.

The challenge now is to make these technologies affordable and widely available, particularly in developing economies where much of the world's new infrastructure will be built.

articles.personality_title_es: COP31 impulsa iniciativas verdes en IA e industria pese a difíciles negociaciones climáticas
